title: Viral Dhokla Chaat Is the Diwali Party Starter You Need
excerpt: Pooja Purohit's instant besan dhokla, steamed for 12-15 minutes and layered over yoghurt and chutneys with sev and pomegranate, gets a full chaat makeover for Diwali parties.
body:
• Content creator Pooja Purohit gives instant dhokla a chaat makeover for Diwali, layering steamed dhokla over whisked yoghurt and green and tamarind chutneys.
  • The dhokla batter uses 1 cup besan, 3/4 cup water, turmeric, lemon juice and 1 tsp Eno, steamed for 12-15 minutes before a mustard seed, curry leaf and green chilli tempering.
  • Assembly is finished with chaat masala, roasted cumin powder, sev, pomegranate pearls, coriander and optional boondi, and the bowls are assembled just before serving so the sev stays crunchy.
  • A second dhokla chaat, Sanjeev Kapoor's mug version, uses the same building blocks — gram flour, yoghurt, fruit salt, both chutneys, pomegranate, sev and coriander — cooked in a microwave for 2 minutes per mug.

Diwali parties need a starter that can be made in batches, served quickly and eaten standing up with a spoon. According to NDTV Food, a viral dhokla chaat shared by content creator Pooja Purohit is being pitched for exactly that job this festive season.

The street-style snack combines soft and spongy dhokla with tangy chutneys, creamy yoghurt and crunchy sev, bringing together sweet, spicy and savoury flavours in one bowl. In the caption quoted by NDTV Food, Purohit wrote: “Diwali parties without chaat starters? No way, it’s a MUST !! I thought of making regular instant dhoklas for the Diwali party, but then I thought, let’s give this a chaat makeover, so here it is. This Diwali, do try it out; it’s dhokla and it’s chaat it can never go wrong.”

How the dhokla is made

The base is an instant besan dhokla. Besan is whisked in a large mixing bowl with salt and turmeric powder, then water is poured in gradually while whisking to make a lump-free batter. Oil and lemon juice are mixed in. Just before steaming, Eno fruit salt is added and gently mixed until the batter becomes light and fluffy — that timing matters, because the batter goes straight into greased moulds, filled only about three-fourths of the way, and steams for around 12 to 15 minutes.

Once steamed, the dhokla gets a tempering. Oil is heated in a small pan, mustard seeds are added and allowed to splutter, then curry leaves and slit green chillies are stirred briefly before the heat is turned off. The tempering is poured over the unmoulded dhokla pieces so they absorb the flavours before the chaat is assembled.

Assembling the chaat

Assembly is where a plain dhokla becomes chaat. Serving bowls are lined first with a layer of whisked yoghurt, followed by green chutney and tamarind chutney. The steamed dhokla pieces sit over that base, then chaat masala and roasted cumin powder are sprinkled on top. The finish is generous: sev, pomegranate pearls, boondi and freshly chopped coriander leaves.

The recipe’s one serving instruction is practical for a party. Prepare the bowls just before serving so the dhokla stays soft while the sev retains its crunch, and serve immediately. Making the components ahead — steamed dhokla, tempering, chutneys and whisked yoghurt — and assembling to order keeps that contrast intact for guests.

The same idea, in a mug

The combination itself is not new, which is part of its appeal for home cooks. Sanjeev Kapoor’s Mug Dhokla Chaat describes fluffy spongy dhokla cooked in a mug, topped with sweet and spicy chutneys, fresh pomegranate pearls, masala peanuts, crunchy sev and fresh coriander, and calls it a Gujarati classic served as a tangy snack for four.

That version also starts with gram flour, yoghurt, ginger-green chilli paste and fruit salt, but it cooks a mug of batter in a microwave on high for 2 minutes, cuts it into four pieces in the mug itself, and then drizzles over green chutney and date and tamarind chutney before the pomegranate, peanuts, sev and coriander go on. For a small household Diwali gathering, the mug route offers a single-serving alternative; for a larger party, Purohit’s steamed batch and bowl assembly scale more naturally.

Why it works for a Diwali spread

For diaspora hosts, the dish answers a familiar problem: a vegetarian starter that feels festive without deep-frying. The full ingredients and method are in the recipe card, taken directly from the NDTV Food recipe.

Make the dhokla, pour over the tempering, and keep the bowls unassembled until guests arrive — that is the whole trick.

steps: Take besan in a large mixing bowl. Add salt and turmeric powder.
Gradually pour in water while whisking to make a lump-free batter. Add oil and lemon juice and mix well.
Just before steaming, add Eno to the batter and gently mix until it becomes light and fluffy.
Grease dhokla moulds with oil. Pour the batter into them, filling each mould only about three-fourths of the way. Place them in a steamer and cook for around 12-15 minutes.
Heat oil in a small pan. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add curry leaves and slit green chillies. Stir briefly and turn off the heat.
Remove the steamed dhokla from the moulds and place them on a plate. Pour the prepared tempering over them so that they absorb the flavours.
Take serving bowls and spread a layer of whisked yoghurt at the bottom. Add green chutney and tamarind chutney.
Place the steamed dhokla pieces over the yoghurt and chutneys. Sprinkle chaat masala and roasted cumin powder on top.
Garnish generously with sev, pomegranate pearls, boondi and freshly chopped coriander leaves.
Prepare the bowls just before serving so that the dhokla stays soft while the sev retains its crunch. Serve immediately.
